criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Several issues and stakeholders identified and linked to engineering organisations and professional duty. Stakeholders are listed but the introduction is generic, and the physical-harm vs data-loss distinction is not framed in the introduction. Context is present but thin.

evidence.quote: the relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel’s company, the chip contract company, the government health department
The potential harm to end-users and responsibility of Rachel and the company are key considerations in this decision.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Arguments for shipping are presented but are largely asserted and one-sided; the against side is stronger. Conclusions for stakeholders are mainly for Rachel and company, with limited consideration of the health department or end-users' decision-making. The 'for' case lacks depth on how Rachel should determine when shipping is acceptable.

evidence.quote: Apple Inc. has demonstrated this competitive advantage best through its strategy of regular product releases.
Shipping potentially defective products is not an ethical way to conduct business.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Logical structure is apparent, but the conclusion is internally inconsistent: the conclusion says not to ship while the recommendation says to accept the contract, and the recommendation's conditions are not justified. The argument is not fully compelling.

evidence.quote: Rachel should accept the contract with the government health department.
the decision to Not Ship is certainly the most ethical path.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Uses several external case studies (NHS, Volkswagen) and EACE code references, plus a quantitative illustration. Evidence is relevant but the Apple/CNBC source is weak for the argument, and quantitative analysis is minimal. Reference list is partly incomplete.

evidence.quote: In late 2023, the Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) investigated a series ofIT system failures
If even 1 percent of the 5,000 servers in the contract failed, that would be 500 failed servers in hospitals.

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Has headings and references in IEEE style but no abstract, no figures or tables, and typos (DICUSSION, 'could very well be the difference', 'ofcompetence'). Reference [3] lacks URL and [4] has a garbled author. Limited visual elements and some language issues.

evidence.quote: [3] BBC NEWS, “IT failures causing patient deaths, says NHS safety body,” 20 DEC 2023. [Online]. [Accessed Jun 2024].
Ethics are a critical component to a functioning society.

technical_issues.issue: Recommends accepting the government contract while the conclusion argues Not Ship; the recommendation lacks conditions on when shipping is acceptable, contradicting the overall stance.
Physical-harm versus data-loss distinction required by R1 is not clearly drawn; the 1% failure figure is arbitrary and unsupported.
Claim that NHS incident involved 'almost identical malfunction scenario' overstates the analogy to defective server shipping; causal link to deaths is asserted without qualification.
Abstract missing; the abstract required by the format is absent.

overall: Engages the scenario with relevant external cases and EACE references, but contains a contradictory recommendation, weak handling of the for-shipping case and the physical-harm distinction, missing abstract, and several typos and incomplete references.

feedback.summary: You engaged the scenario well, identifying several stakeholders and drawing on relevant external cases such as the NHS HSSIB investigation and Volkswagen, along with EACE code references. The main gaps are an internal contradiction between your conclusion (Not Ship) and your recommendation (accept the government contract), weak treatment of the case for shipping, and the missing abstract. Addressing these would strengthen the report considerably.
next_steps: Align your recommendation with your conclusion: state explicitly the conditions under which shipping would be acceptable, such as verified fixes, disclosure to the health department, or a risk threshold, and justify them with evidence.
Strengthen the case for shipping by supporting it with evidence rather than assertion, and clearly separate physical-harm risks from data-loss risks, justifying any failure-rate figure you use.
Add the missing abstract, include at least one figure or table to support your analysis, and complete all references with full details, including URLs and accessed dates.

criteria.C1: You identified several relevant ethical issues and linked them to engineering design and professional duty, earning Very good. To reach Excellent, deepen the link between the issues and the design context, and explain how each stakeholder's interests differ (for example, the health department versus end-users). Introducing the physical-harm versus data-loss distinction in your introduction would also help.
criteria.C2: You presented arguments on both sides, but the case for shipping is largely asserted and your discussion is weighted towards the case against. To reach Excellent, give the arguments for shipping real depth, and provide decision-making recommendations for several stakeholders, not mainly Rachel and her company.
criteria.C3: Your report has a logical structure, but the conclusion and recommendation conflict, which weakens the overall argument. Resolve this contradiction and ensure every paragraph links clearly to the conclusion. This would make your argument more compelling and move you towards Very good or Excellent.
criteria.C4: You used relevant external case studies and EACE references, with some quantitative illustration, earning Very good. To reach Excellent, substantiate your figures properly, such as justifying the 1% failure assumption, add a balanced range of qualitative and quantitative evidence, and use stronger sources for the Apple argument. Also qualify the link between the NHS incident and your scenario more carefully.
criteria.C5: Your report uses clear headings and IEEE-style references, but it lacks an abstract, figures or tables, and contains several typos and language errors. Add the abstract, use visual elements to support your discussion, proofread carefully, and complete the incomplete references to reach a higher level.
